title: Given strings s and t, count the number of distinct subsequences of s that equal t.
shortTitle: Distinct Subsequences: count occurrences of t as a subsequence of s
keyPoints: Define dp[i][j] as the number of ways the first i characters of s form the first j characters of t.
When s[i-1] == t[j-1], dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] (use it) + dp[i-1][j] (skip it).
When characters differ, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] (skip only).
Base case: dp[i][0] = 1 for all i, because the empty target is always matchable once.
Space reduces from O(m*n) to O(n) by iterating j from high to low on a single row.
Counts can overflow int on large inputs, so use long or modular arithmetic in production.

s1_definition.oneliner: Match: use + skip (diagonal + above); mismatch: skip only (above). dp[i][0] = 1.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Distinct Subsequences** – count the number of ways to delete characters from string s to produce string t.
- **DP definition** – `dp[i][j]` is the number of ways the first `i` characters of s form the first `j` characters of t.
- **Match transition** – `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + dp[i-1][j]` (use the character or skip it).
- **Mismatch transition** – `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j]` (can only skip).
- **Base case** – `dp[i][0] = 1` for all i; the empty target is matchable exactly once.
- **Complexity** – O(m * n) time, O(n) space with a single row.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a pattern-counter counts how many times a short approval code appears as an ordered subsequence inside a long audit log. At each log character matching the next code character, Priya either uses it or skips it, adding both counts.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Example: s = "rabbbit", t = "rabbit"

     ""  r  a  b  b  i  t
 ""   1  0  0  0  0  0  0
  r   1  1  0  0  0  0  0
  a   1  1  1  0  0  0  0
  b   1  1  1  1  0  0  0
  b   1  1  1  2  1  0  0
  b   1  1  1  3  3  0  0
  i   1  1  1  3  3  3  0
  t   1  1  1  3  3  3  3  ← answer

Match: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + dp[i-1][j]
  (use character)    (skip character)

Mismatch: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j]
  (skip only)

The 3 distinct subsequences of "rabbbit" that form "rabbit":
  r a b b i t  (using b at index 2 and 3)
  r a b b i t  (using b at index 2 and 4)
  r a b b i t  (using b at index 3 and 4)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Distinct Subsequences is a two-dimensional counting DP. I define dp[i][j] as the number of ways the first i characters of the source form the first j characters of the target. The base case is dp[i][0] = 1 for all i, because the empty target is always matchable once.

When the current source character matches the current target character, I have two choices: use it (contributing the diagonal cell) or skip it (contributing the cell above). When they differ, I can only skip. The answer is dp[m][n]. The space-optimised version uses a single row iterated right to left.

The critical implementation detail is the iteration direction: right to left in the space-optimised version preserves the previous row's values. The common mistake is iterating left to right, which overwrites dp[j-1] before it is read. Counts can overflow `int` on large inputs, so use `long`.

At the National Bank of India, an audit tool counted how many times a short approval code appeared as an ordered subsequence in a long transaction log, gauging the number of potential approval chains.

Remember one sentence: match means use-plus-skip from the diagonal and above; mismatch means skip-only from above.
